I am 67 years old, never went to school, and have farmed these same fields in Quzhou for over 50 years. My wife and I manage about 8 mu of land — my children work in the city, so it is just us two now. I do not read or write, but I know my land and I watch what my neighbors do. Every year I grow winter wheat and then summer maize on the same fields. That is what everyone in my village has always done, and the grain buyers come reliably. I am too old to gamble on new crops; if I fail, I have no salary to fall back on.

For the wheat, I will rotary till the soil before planting in early October. I will buy the improved wheat variety from the village shop — the same kind my neighbor across the road plants, the one in the red bag. I cannot tell you exactly how many kilograms, but I put down about two bags of compound fertilizer per mu before sowing, and another half-bag of ammonium bicarbonate if I have the cash. I will irrigate four times: after sowing, at green-up, at jointing, and when the grain is filling. Water from the well costs money, but I have seen what happens when you skip irrigation — the yield drops by half. I will spray pesticides three times when I see aphids or weeds.

For the maize, I plant immediately after the wheat harvest in mid-June. There is no time to till the soil — barely one week between harvest and planting — so I sow directly into the wheat stubble. I use a hybrid maize seed; it grows fast and strong. I spread one bag of high-nitrogen compound fertilizer per mu. The maize needs less water than wheat, so I irrigate twice, three times only if the summer is very dry. Two pesticide sprays are enough — one for weeds and one for the corn borers that come in August.

I expect about 500 kg per mu of wheat and about 550 kg per mu of maize. Last year I got roughly that much. I do not want to risk changing anything.
